Offline embedding refresh jobs are scheduled batch processes that regenerate vector embeddings for a corpus when conditions trigger a need to update the vectors — typically when the underlying embedding model changes or source documents update in bulk.

## Execution Model

Rather than running on demand or in real time, these jobs run on a **fixed cadence** (e.g. daily, weekly), re-embedding the full corpus or an incremental set of updated documents. This predictable schedule allows for easier resource planning and avoids the operational complexity of handling concurrent embedding tasks.

## Index Atomicity

A critical safety mechanism is the **atomic swap** of vectors into the retrieval index. New embeddings are staged separately, then swapped in as a single operation to avoid serving a state where old and new vectors coexist. This prevents quality degradation mid-transition — e.g. semantic drift from serving results from a mix of embedding models.

## Operational Concerns

### Model Versioning
Each batch must track which embedding model version produced its vectors. This versioning enables:
- Debugging mismatches between embedding and retrieval logic
- Rolling back to a prior version if quality suffers
- Monitoring which documents were embedded with which model

### Drift Detection
Monitoring the **drift between old and new vectors** is essential to catch regressions early. This can include:
- Distance metrics between old and new embeddings for the same document
- Query result shifts after a swap
- Relevance metrics over time

### Blue-Green Index Staging
A **blue-green deployment** strategy for the index allows a new embedding batch to be prepared in a shadow index before being promoted to serve live traffic. If quality regresses after the swap, rolling back to the previous (blue) index is straightforward — a single pointer flip — without needing to re-embed the corpus again.
